name: Super BIMAX

lead: Super BIMAX is looksmax.org shorthand for a bimaxillary advancement taken further than usual, moving the upper and lower jaws forward by larger distances to give a more projected midface and chin. The goal is a stronger profile and, for some, improved airway.

A thread titled for a roughly 30 mm result circulates in the community, with members commenting on facial widening and the upper face. No clinical series using the term was found; standard double-jaw surgery is described in orthognathic literature.

paras: Bimaxillary surgery is performed by oral and maxillofacial surgeons: the upper jaw is cut and moved (Le Fort I) and the lower jaw is split and moved (BSSO), then fixed with plates, followed by weeks of liquid diet and healing.

Orthognathic surgery carries risks of bleeding, swelling, infection, and nerve damage causing numbness that usually improves over about three months. Larger movements are a topic for surgical assessment.

angle.text: Moving both jaws forward changes bone position and therefore profile. The 'super' label refers to a larger advancement than usual.

lead: Super BIMAX is a looksmax.org term for an extended bimaxillary advancement, in which both jaws are moved forward further than in a typical double-jaw operation [1]. Bimaxillary surgery generally pairs an upper-jaw osteotomy with a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy of the lower jaw [2].

The appeal is facial projection: advancing the maxilla and mandible changes the profile, the chin and the lower face. In the thread, posters react to a before-and-after showing about 30 mm and note the face looks wider, and one points out the upper midface was not advanced [1].
The term has no formal clinical definition.
infobox: Upper jaw osteotomy plus bilateral sagittal split of lower jaw [2]
About 2-6 weeks; bone union a further 2-4 months [2]

paras: The term appears in a looksmax.org thread about a roughly 30 mm advancement, where members discuss the visible widening of the face and that the upper midface was not included [1]. Orthognathic surgery in general corrects skeletal discrepancies, bite problems, asymmetry and obstructive sleep apnea, and surgery on both jaws is usual [2].

Reported complications of jaw surgery include bleeding, swelling, infection (up to 7%), and nerve damage with numbness that usually recovers within about three months [2]. Jaws may be immobilised for 1-4 weeks, patients often follow a liquid diet and lose weight, and return to work takes 2-6 weeks [2]. Software prediction is used to plan facial change [2].
No studies found using the term. General orthognathic surgery is described in Wikipedia: one cited 50-patient study reports 90-100% success for sleep apnea [2].
